setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: A 25-year-old with acute asthma is drowsy, has a silent chest and SpO2 89% on oxygen. Arterial blood gas shows PaCO2 46 mmHg. How should this exacerbation be classified?

options.A: Moderate asthma suitable for ward management with regular nebulised bronchodilators
options.C: Mild asthma; discharge with oral steroids
options.E: Near-fatal (life-threatening) asthma needing ICU review and likely ventilation

explanation: A normal or raised PaCO2 in acute asthma indicates fatigue and impending respiratory failure, since patients usually hyperventilate. Silent chest, drowsiness, cyanosis and SpO2 below 92% are life-threatening features requiring urgent senior and ICU involvement.

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: A patient with acute severe asthma fails to respond to repeated nebulised salbutamol, ipratropium and IV hydrocortisone. Which IV therapy is recommended next?

options.C: Aminophylline 5 mg/kg bolus in a patient on oral theophylline
options.D: Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 20 minutes

explanation: IV magnesium (2 g over 20 minutes) is recommended for severe exacerbations not responding to initial therapy; it causes bronchial smooth muscle relaxation. Aminophylline adds toxicity with little benefit and a loading dose must be avoided in patients on theophylline.

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: Which initial ventilator strategy is most appropriate for a patient intubated for status asthmaticus?

options.B: Low rate (10–12/min), tidal volume 6–8 mL/kg PBW, high inspiratory flow, permissive hypercapnia
options.C: High respiratory rate (25/min) with normal tidal volume to normalise the PaCO2 and pH quickly
options.D: Tidal volume of 12 mL/kg to recruit alveoli
options.E: PEEP of 15 cmH2O with a long inspiratory pause to keep the small airways open

explanation: The aim is to minimise dynamic hyperinflation by reducing minute ventilation and maximising expiratory time (I:E 1:4 or more), accepting hypercapnia if pH remains acceptable. Plateau pressure should be kept below about 30 cmH2O and intrinsic PEEP monitored.
referenceText: GINA 2024 report [78]; Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: A patient with severe asthma receiving continuous salbutamol nebulisation and IV salbutamol develops lactate of 6 mmol/L with clinical improvement in airflow. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Beta-2 agonist-induced type B lactic acidosis
options.C: Respiratory muscle fatigue with hypoxia in all cases

explanation: High-dose beta-2 agonists stimulate glycogenolysis and glycolysis, causing type B lactic acidosis. It may increase respiratory rate and be mistaken for worsening asthma; reducing beta-agonist dose usually resolves it.

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: Which drug is often used as an induction and sedative agent in intubated patients with severe bronchospasm because of its bronchodilator properties?
explanation: Ketamine has sympathomimetic bronchodilating effects and maintains haemodynamic stability, making it useful for induction and sedation in severe asthma. Morphine and atracurium release histamine, and non-selective beta-blockers and neostigmine may worsen bronchospasm.
referenceText: GINA 2024 report [78]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: What duration of systemic corticosteroids is recommended for most hospitalised COPD exacerbations?
explanation: GOLD recommends prednisolone 40 mg daily for 5 days; the REDUCE trial showed 5 days was non-inferior to 14 days for re-exacerbation, with lower steroid exposure. Longer courses increase hyperglycaemia, infection and myopathy.

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: In an acute COPD exacerbation, which feature most supports antibiotic therapy?

options.C: Normal sputum colour and no change in volume, but a raised CRP and white cell count on admission
options.E: Increased sputum purulence plus more dyspnoea or sputum volume, or need for ventilation

explanation: GOLD recommends antibiotics when there is increased sputum purulence plus increased dyspnoea or sputum volume, or when invasive or non-invasive ventilation is needed. Antibiotics reduce treatment failure and mortality in ventilated patients.

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: A ventilated patient with COPD has hypotension and measured intrinsic PEEP of 12 cmH2O. Which ventilator change is most helpful?

options.A: Increase the respiratory rate to normalise PaCO2 to 40 mmHg and correct acidosis
options.B: Lower rate and tidal volume to reduce minute ventilation and lengthen expiration
options.E: Add an inspiratory pause of 1 second

explanation: Intrinsic PEEP results from incomplete emptying; reducing minute ventilation is the most effective way to reduce it. Many COPD patients have chronic hypercapnia, so PaCO2 should be targeted to the patient's baseline (pH normal) rather than 40 mmHg.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]; GOLD 2025 report [79]

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: A patient with confirmed PE has BP 128/76 mmHg, a dilated RV on CT and elevated troponin, with sPESI of 2. How is this PE classified by the ESC?
explanation: ESC 2019 classifies normotensive PE with sPESI ≥1 (or PESI III–V), plus both RV dysfunction on imaging and elevated troponin, as intermediate-high risk. These patients receive anticoagulation and close monitoring, with rescue reperfusion if haemodynamic decompensation occurs.

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: What did the PEITHO trial show for systemic tenecteplase in intermediate-risk PE?

options.A: Less haemodynamic decompensation but more major bleeding and stroke, with no mortality benefit
options.B: Benefit greatest in patients over 75 years
options.C: Reduced major bleeding compared with heparin alone, together with a fall in 30-day mortality

explanation: PEITHO showed that tenecteplase reduced the combined outcome of death or haemodynamic decompensation within 7 days, mainly through less decompensation, but increased major extracranial bleeding and haemorrhagic stroke (2% vs 0.2%). ESC recommends against routine thrombolysis in intermediate-risk PE.
referenceText: Meyer et al. 2014 (PEITHO) [139]; Konstantinides et al. 2020 (ESC pulmonary embolism) [117]

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: A patient with confirmed PE has BP 75/50 mmHg despite fluids and noradrenaline, with no contraindications to thrombolysis. What is recommended?

options.B: Systemic thrombolysis (e.g. alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours) with heparin
options.D: Wait for repeat echocardiography in 24 hours while continuing noradrenaline

explanation: High-risk PE (shock or persistent hypotension) requires immediate reperfusion. ESC recommends systemic thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours, or 0.6 mg/kg over 15 minutes in an accelerated regimen) with UFH. Surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed therapy are alternatives if thrombolysis is contraindicated or fails.

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: A patient 5 days after craniotomy develops high-risk PE with shock. What is the most appropriate reperfusion approach?

options.A: Low-molecular-weight heparin alone with close observation

explanation: Recent intracranial surgery is an absolute contraindication to systemic thrombolysis. ESC recommends surgical pulmonary embolectomy or catheter-directed treatment for high-risk PE when thrombolysis is contraindicated or has failed.

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: For a normotensive patient with intermediate-high-risk PE, which anticoagulant is preferred initially in the first 2–3 days?

options.B: No anticoagulation until the troponin normalises and RV function improves
options.D: LMWH, or unfractionated heparin if rescue reperfusion may be needed

explanation: ESC recommends parenteral anticoagulation (LMWH or fondaparinux preferred over UFH) in most patients; UFH is preferred if reperfusion is being considered, in severe renal impairment or in severe obesity because it is short-acting and reversible. NOACs are suitable for most patients once stable.

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: Which test strategy is recommended for diagnosing PE in a haemodynamically unstable patient who cannot be safely transferred to CT?

options.D: Ventilation–perfusion scan in the nuclear medicine department

explanation: In suspected high-risk PE, bedside echocardiography is recommended; the absence of RV dysfunction essentially excludes PE as the cause of shock, while its presence justifies reperfusion if CTPA cannot be performed. D-dimer is for low or intermediate probability patients.

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: How is the age-adjusted D-dimer cut-off calculated for patients older than 50 years?

options.E: A fixed 500 µg/L regardless of age

explanation: For patients over 50 years, the age-adjusted cut-off (age × 10 µg/L) increases specificity while preserving sensitivity, allowing safe exclusion of PE in more older patients with non-high clinical probability.

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: Which echocardiographic sign is relatively specific for acute PE?

options.A: McConnell sign (RV free-wall hypokinesia, apical sparing)
options.E: Left ventricular hypertrophy with diastolic dysfunction and E/e′ >14

explanation: The McConnell sign and the 60/60 sign (pulmonary acceleration time below 60 ms with tricuspid regurgitation gradient below 60 mmHg) are relatively specific for acute PE, though insensitive. RV dilatation (RV/LV ratio above 1) indicates RV pressure overload.

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: In which situation is an IVC filter indicated in acute PE?

options.A: Anticoagulation absolutely contraindicated, or PE recurring despite it
options.B: Before any surgery in patients on warfarin
options.D: In addition to anticoagulation in all patients with active cancer and DVT
options.E: Routine use in all patients with intermediate-risk PE

explanation: ESC recommends IVC filters only for patients with acute PE and absolute contraindications to anticoagulation, or recurrence despite adequate anticoagulation. Routine use does not reduce mortality (PREPIC 2) and filters increase DVT.

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: According to ATLS 10th edition, what is the preferred site for needle decompression of a tension pneumothorax in adults?

options.A: The fifth intercostal space just anterior to the midaxillary line
options.B: The second intercostal space in the posterior axillary line
options.C: The fourth intercostal space at the left sternal edge
options.D: The eighth intercostal space in the scapular line

explanation: ATLS 10th edition recommends needle decompression at the fifth intercostal space slightly anterior to the midaxillary line in adults, because the chest wall is thinner there, improving success. The second intercostal space in the midclavicular line is an alternative; definitive treatment is a chest drain.
referenceText: ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]; Roberts et al. 2023 (BTS pleural disease) [180]

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: A ventilated patient develops a moderate pneumothorax without haemodynamic compromise. What is the appropriate management?

options.C: Observation with repeat radiograph in 24 hours
options.E: Increase PEEP to tamponade the leak

explanation: Positive pressure ventilation can rapidly convert a simple pneumothorax into tension physiology, so pneumothoraces in ventilated patients are treated with a chest drain. Conservative or aspiration-only strategies are used for selected spontaneous pneumothoraces in non-ventilated patients.

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: Which lung ultrasound sign is most specific for pneumothorax?
explanation: The lung point is the boundary where sliding lung meets the pneumothorax and has near 100% specificity. Absent lung sliding is sensitive but non-specific (seen with apnoea, mainstem intubation, pleurodesis). The presence of lung sliding or B-lines excludes pneumothorax at that point.
referenceText: Volpicelli et al. 2012 (lung ultrasound recommendations) [230]; Lichtenstein & Mezière 2008 (BLUE protocol) [130]

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: A patient with pneumonia has a pleural effusion with pH 7.08, glucose 1.8 mmol/L and no pus. What is the most appropriate management?

options.D: Insert a chest drain, as this is a complicated parapneumonic effusion
options.E: Antibiotics alone, with repeat chest imaging in 2 weeks to confirm resolution

explanation: BTS guidance recommends chest drainage for pleural infection when fluid is purulent, pleural pH is below 7.2, or glucose is very low, or there is a positive Gram stain or culture. Antibiotics alone fail in complicated effusions.

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: A patient with loculated empyema has persistent sepsis despite a chest drain and antibiotics, and is not fit for surgery. What intrapleural therapy has been shown to improve drainage?

options.D: Saline irrigation alone through the existing drain
options.E: Tissue plasminogen activator combined with DNase

explanation: MIST2 showed that combined intrapleural tPA and DNase improved radiographic pleural opacity and reduced surgical referral and hospital stay, whereas either agent alone was ineffective. Surgical options (VATS) are considered when drainage fails.
referenceText: Rahman et al. 2011 (MIST2) [174]; Roberts et al. 2023 (BTS pleural disease) [180]

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: After insertion of a chest drain for a large malignant effusion, 2.8 L is drained over 30 minutes, and the patient develops cough, chest tightness and hypoxaemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Rapid drainage of large effusions or pneumothoraces can cause re-expansion pulmonary oedema. BTS recommends limiting drainage to about 1.5 L at a time and stopping if symptoms such as cough or chest discomfort occur.

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: After a stab wound to the chest, a chest drain immediately drains 1700 mL of blood. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Give tranexamic acid and observe only
options.D: Observe for 6 hours and repeat radiograph
options.E: Clamp the chest drain to tamponade bleeding

explanation: ATLS indications for thoracotomy include initial drainage of ≥1500 mL of blood, or ongoing loss of 200 mL/h for 2–4 hours, or persistent need for transfusion. Clamping the drain may produce tension haemothorax.

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: After oesophagectomy, a patient's chest drain output becomes milky, about 1.5 L/day. Pleural triglyceride is 4.0 mmol/L (354 mg/dL). What is the diagnosis?
explanation: Chylothorax is confirmed by pleural triglycerides above 1.24 mmol/L (110 mg/dL) or the presence of chylomicrons. Thoracic duct injury after oesophagectomy is a classic cause. Management includes drainage, nil by mouth or medium-chain triglyceride diet, octreotide and surgical ligation for high-output leaks.
referenceText: Roberts et al. 2023 (BTS pleural disease) [180]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: Which finding classifies a pleural effusion as an exudate by Light's criteria?

options.B: Pleural fluid to serum protein ratio above 0.5
options.C: Pleural protein of 15 g/L with serum protein 70 g/L
options.D: Pleural fluid to serum LDH ratio below 0.6
options.E: Pleural fluid LDH below two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH

explanation: An effusion is an exudate if any one Light's criterion is met: pleural/serum protein ratio above 0.5, pleural/serum LDH ratio above 0.6, or pleural LDH above two-thirds the upper limit of normal serum LDH. Diuretic-treated heart failure may produce false exudates.

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: A patient with bronchiectasis has massive haemoptysis from the right lung with hypoxaemia. Before definitive treatment, which positioning is most appropriate?

options.C: Lateral decubitus with the bleeding (right) side down
options.E: Sitting upright with the head flexed to aid coughing

explanation: Placing the bleeding lung dependent prevents spillage of blood into the healthy lung. Airway protection may involve intubation with a large single-lumen tube advanced into the left (non-bleeding) main bronchus or a double-lumen tube, followed by bronchoscopy and bronchial artery embolisation.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]; Marino 2014 (The ICU Book, 4th ed.) [131]

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: What is the source of bleeding in most cases of massive haemoptysis, and the preferred definitive non-surgical treatment?

options.C: The bronchial arteries; bronchial artery embolisation

explanation: About 90% of massive haemoptysis arises from the high-pressure bronchial arterial circulation, which hypertrophies in chronic inflammation (bronchiectasis, tuberculosis, aspergilloma). Bronchial artery embolisation controls bleeding in most patients; surgery is reserved for failure or specific lesions.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: Which finding is a major criterion for severe community-acquired pneumonia according to ATS/IDSA 2007, as used in the 2019 guideline?
explanation: ATS/IDSA define severe CAP by one of two major criteria (septic shock needing vasopressors, or respiratory failure needing mechanical ventilation) or three or more minor criteria (respiratory rate ≥30, PaO2/FiO2 ≤250, multilobar infiltrates, confusion, uraemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, hypothermia, hypotension requiring aggressive fluids).

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: A 70-year-old woman with pneumonia is alert, with urea 8.5 mmol/L, respiratory rate 24/min and BP 95/60 mmHg. What is her CURB-65 score?
explanation: CURB-65 assigns 1 point each for confusion, urea above 7 mmol/L, respiratory rate ≥30/min, systolic BP below 90 or diastolic ≤60 mmHg, and age ≥65 years. She scores urea 1, diastolic BP 60 = 1, age 1, total 3, indicating severe pneumonia requiring hospital and consideration of higher-level care.
referenceText: Metlay et al. 2019 (ATS/IDSA community-acquired pneumonia) [138]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: What empirical antibiotic regimen is recommended for severe CAP in ICU without risk factors for MRSA or Pseudomonas?

options.C: A beta-lactam (e.g. ceftriaxone) plus a macrolide
options.D: Vancomycin plus meropenem in all patients

explanation: ATS/IDSA 2019 recommend a beta-lactam plus a macrolide, or a beta-lactam plus a respiratory fluoroquinolone, for severe CAP. MRSA or Pseudomonas coverage is added only with prior isolation or validated local risk factors.

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: What did the CAPE COD trial show for hydrocortisone in severe community-acquired pneumonia?

options.B: Increased gastrointestinal bleeding, leading to early trial termination
options.E: Reduced 28-day mortality, with less intubation and vasopressor use

explanation: CAPE COD randomised 800 ICU patients with severe CAP (excluding septic shock and influenza) to hydrocortisone 200 mg/day for 4–8 days with taper, or placebo. Mortality at 28 days fell from 11.9% to 6.2%. The 2024 SCCM update recommends corticosteroids for severe bacterial CAP.
referenceText: Dequin et al. 2023 (CAPE COD) [52]; Chaudhuri et al. 2024 (SCCM corticosteroid update) [35]

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: A patient with severe pneumonia has diarrhoea, confusion, Na+ 126 mmol/L and raised liver enzymes after a hotel stay. Which test is most useful for rapid diagnosis?
explanation: Legionnaires' disease is associated with hyponatraemia, gastrointestinal symptoms, confusion and liver dysfunction. Urinary antigen detects L. pneumophila serogroup 1 rapidly; PCR of respiratory samples increases sensitivity. Treatment is with a macrolide or fluoroquinolone.
referenceText: Metlay et al. 2019 (ATS/IDSA community-acquired pneumonia) [138]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: A patient admitted to ICU with severe influenza A pneumonia has had symptoms for 5 days. What is the recommendation regarding oseltamivir?

options.A: Start only after viral culture results
options.C: Withhold oseltamivir because symptoms exceed 48 hours
options.D: Give oseltamivir only if the patient is immunocompromised or pregnant
options.E: Start oseltamivir as soon as possible, whatever the symptom duration

explanation: IDSA recommends antiviral treatment as soon as possible for hospitalised patients with influenza, regardless of illness duration, because observational data show benefit even when started after 48 hours. Amantadine is not recommended because of resistance.

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: A patient with a witnessed aspiration of gastric contents during an alcohol-related seizure develops hypoxaemia and bilateral infiltrates within 2 hours. What is the most appropriate initial approach regarding antibiotics?

options.A: Bronchoalveolar lavage with saline to neutralise acid
options.D: Immediate broad-spectrum antibiotics with anaerobic coverage for a full 14-day course in all cases
options.E: Supportive care; antibiotics are not routine for chemical pneumonitis unless infection develops

explanation: Aspiration pneumonitis is a chemical injury caused by gastric acid. Antibiotics are not routinely indicated early; they are considered if symptoms persist or features of bacterial pneumonia develop. Steroids and lavage are not beneficial; ATS/IDSA 2019 suggest against routine anaerobic coverage for suspected aspiration pneumonia.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]; Metlay et al. 2019 (ATS/IDSA community-acquired pneumonia) [138]

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: A patient with known pulmonary arterial hypertension is admitted with sepsis and hypotension. Which factor most worsens RV afterload and should be avoided?

options.E: Maintenance of systemic blood pressure with noradrenaline

explanation: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, hypercapnia and acidaemia increase pulmonary vascular resistance and can precipitate RV failure. Management includes optimising oxygenation, avoiding excessive intrathoracic pressure, maintaining systemic pressure for RV coronary perfusion, and continuing pulmonary vasodilators.
referenceText: Konstantinides et al. 2020 (ESC pulmonary embolism) [117]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: A patient with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis has an acute exacerbation with severe hypoxaemia. Why is invasive ventilation often not recommended?

options.A: These patients respond well to high PEEP
options.B: IPF exacerbations always resolve with high-flow oxygen and pulsed steroids within a few days
options.D: Ventilation mortality is very high unless there is a reversible cause or transplant plan
options.E: Ventilation is contraindicated because of airway obstruction

explanation: Acute exacerbations of IPF carry high mortality, and outcomes of invasive ventilation are poor (hospital mortality often above 80%). Decisions should consider reversibility, transplant eligibility and patient wishes, with advance care planning ideally before crises.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: A patient with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis requires intubation. Which infection-control measure is most important?

options.B: Airborne precautions: negative-pressure room, N95/FFP3 respirator and a circuit filter
options.D: Droplet precautions only, with surgical masks and eye protection for all staff in the room

explanation: TB is transmitted by airborne droplet nuclei; airborne isolation, respirators, closed suction and expiratory filters protect staff. Aerosol-generating procedures such as intubation and bronchoscopy increase transmission risk.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: A woman at 30 weeks of gestation is suspected of having PE; she is haemodynamically stable with a normal chest radiograph and no signs of DVT on compression ultrasound. Which imaging is reasonable?

options.A: CT pulmonary angiography or perfusion scan; both give low fetal radiation
options.C: Pulmonary angiography via the femoral vein, with abdominal lead shielding

explanation: ESC suggests CTPA or perfusion lung scan in pregnancy; both have fetal radiation doses well below harmful thresholds. A normal chest radiograph favours perfusion scanning. LMWH is the anticoagulant of choice; DOACs and warfarin (in the first trimester) are avoided.

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: Which corticosteroid regimen is recommended for adults hospitalised with acute severe asthma?

options.A: No steroids if salbutamol is effective
options.B: Dexamethasone 20 mg daily for 21 days, then a slow taper
options.C: Prednisolone 40–50 mg daily (or IV equivalent) for 5–7 days

explanation: GINA recommends systemic corticosteroids early in moderate and severe exacerbations, typically prednisolone 40–50 mg daily for 5–7 days; oral and IV routes are equally effective when the patient can swallow. Steroids reduce relapse and hospitalisation.

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: Which history feature most increases the risk of asthma-related death?

options.D: Use of inhaled corticosteroids as maintenance

explanation: Risk factors for asthma death include previous near-fatal asthma requiring intubation, recent hospitalisation, overuse of short-acting beta-agonists, not using inhaled corticosteroids, psychiatric illness and poor adherence. These patients need early aggressive treatment.

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: Which mechanism is the main cause of hypoxaemia in acute PE?

options.C: Diffusion limitation from thickened alveolar membranes and interstitial oedema fluid
options.D: V/Q mismatch from flow redistribution to normal lung, sometimes with PFO shunting

explanation: Obstruction redistributes pulmonary blood flow to non-occluded areas, creating low V/Q regions; low cardiac output lowers mixed venous oxygen, and raised right atrial pressure may open a PFO. Patients are usually hypocapnic from hyperventilation.
referenceText: Konstantinides et al. 2020 (ESC pulmonary embolism) [117]; Marino 2014 (The ICU Book, 4th ed.) [131]

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: In which PE patient is catheter-directed therapy most appropriate?

options.B: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension in all patients at the time of diagnosis
options.D: High-risk PE with thrombolysis contraindicated or failed, at an expert centre

explanation: ESC recommends percutaneous catheter-directed treatment (or surgical embolectomy) for high-risk PE when thrombolysis is contraindicated or has failed, and suggests it for intermediate-high-risk patients who deteriorate on anticoagulation. Its role in routine intermediate-risk PE is under investigation.

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: A patient with severe COPD presents with dyspnoea and a 3 cm rim right pneumothorax. What is the recommended management?

options.A: Oxygen and observation only regardless of symptoms
options.D: Thoracic surgery as the first step in all cases
options.E: Chest drain insertion and hospital admission

explanation: Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax in patients with underlying lung disease is poorly tolerated, with higher mortality. Symptomatic or larger secondary pneumothoraces usually need chest drainage and admission; surgical referral is considered for persistent air leak or recurrence.

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: A previously healthy young man develops severe necrotising pneumonia with haemoptysis and cavitation after an influenza-like illness. Which organism should be covered empirically?

options.A: Chlamydophila pneumoniae after secondary viral infection

explanation: Post-influenza necrotising pneumonia with haemoptysis and leucopenia suggests PVL-producing S. aureus. Empirical therapy should include anti-MRSA coverage (vancomycin or linezolid) plus a toxin-suppressing agent such as clindamycin or linezolid.

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: A ventilated patient has a large pleural effusion on ultrasound with difficult oxygenation. Which statement about drainage is most accurate?

options.A: Ultrasound-guided drainage is safe when ventilated and may improve oxygenation
options.C: Thoracentesis is contraindicated during mechanical ventilation with any level of PEEP
options.D: Drainage should be performed blind to avoid delay

explanation: Ultrasound guidance reduces complications of thoracentesis, which can be safely performed in ventilated patients. Drainage of large effusions may improve oxygenation and respiratory mechanics, though the effect on outcome is uncertain.
referenceText: Roberts et al. 2023 (BTS pleural disease) [180]; Volpicelli et al. 2012 (lung ultrasound recommendations) [230]

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: Which is an absolute contraindication to systemic thrombolysis for PE?

options.D: Oral anticoagulant therapy with a normal INR
options.E: Ischaemic stroke within the previous 6 months

explanation: ESC absolute contraindications include previous haemorrhagic stroke or stroke of unknown origin, ischaemic stroke within 6 months, CNS neoplasm, major trauma, surgery or head injury within 3 weeks, bleeding diathesis and active bleeding. Age over 75, pregnancy, anticoagulant use and traumatic CPR are relative contraindications.

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: In acute severe asthma, which statement about adrenaline is correct?

options.A: IV adrenaline is the first-line bronchodilator for all exacerbations
options.B: Intramuscular adrenaline is indicated for asthma with anaphylaxis or angio-oedema
options.D: Adrenaline should never be used in asthma
options.E: Subcutaneous adrenaline is preferred over inhaled salbutamol in adults with asthma

explanation: GINA reserves adrenaline for acute asthma associated with anaphylaxis and angio-oedema; inhaled short-acting beta-agonists are first line. IV adrenaline or salbutamol may be used in refractory life-threatening asthma in monitored settings.

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: Which measurement is most useful for monitoring dynamic hyperinflation in a passive ventilated patient with severe asthma?

options.B: Respiratory rate and minute ventilation displayed on the ventilator
options.D: Plateau pressure and intrinsic PEEP from inspiratory and expiratory holds

explanation: Peak pressure largely reflects airway resistance and does not indicate the degree of hyperinflation. Plateau pressure (target below about 30 cmH2O) and intrinsic PEEP (ideally below about 10 cmH2O) better reflect end-inspiratory and end-expiratory lung volumes and the risk of barotrauma and hypotension.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]; GINA 2024 report [78]

setTitle: Asthma, COPD, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleural Disease and
stem: A patient with clinically and radiologically confirmed CAP has a low serum procalcitonin. What do the ATS/IDSA 2019 guidelines recommend?

options.A: Treat only if procalcitonin exceeds 2 ng/mL
options.B: Withhold antibiotics because the procalcitonin level is low
options.C: Start empirical antibiotics regardless of the initial procalcitonin
options.E: Repeat procalcitonin in 24 hours before deciding

explanation: ATS/IDSA recommend empirical antibiotic therapy for adults with clinically suspected and radiographically confirmed CAP regardless of initial procalcitonin, because low values do not reliably exclude bacterial infection. Procalcitonin may be more useful in guiding duration.
